monogr.title: George Ashby's Active Policy of a Prince and Dicta et Opiniones Diversorum Philosophorum

projectDesc.p: The Middle English Texts Series offers a diverse and representative array of literary texts that medieval readers in the present-day British Isles would have encountered between the twelfth and sixteenth centuries. It is committed to making available both affordable print and open access editions to scholars, teachers, and students of the Western Middle Ages. In its digital publications, the series prioritizes a user-friendly interface and viewing options, multiple downloadable formats, enhanced searchability and filtering, and accessibility to the widest possible range of users.

editorialDecl.p: METS takes as its mission the creation of affordable editions that would pass scrutiny from the most demanding expert, yet would prove comprehensible, and even enticing, to someone who had never read Middle English before. This agenda dictates that METS publications offer not a critical edition reflecting all surviving manuscripts, and certainly not a diplomatic edition, but a best-text edition, informed by the notes and apparatus of earlier editions (where these exist), and by substantive variants from other manuscript witnesses. Transcriptions of Middle English texts are lightly modernized to ensure a smooth reading experience, while non-English texts preserve both the original language and a modern English translation in facing-page format. Each edition offers expert assistance with language and lexicon, providing glosses alongside the text(s), textual and explanatory notes, elucidation of unfamiliar contexts and traditions, and thematic and interpretive possibilities. All editions feature general introductions that set the edited text within its own time, place, and traditions, and link it to ancestor, congener, and successor materials. All publications contain comprehensive, current bibliographies of pertinent scholarship and criticism. House style is adapted from the Chicago Manual of Style.

correction.p: This text may include corrections made after the original edition went to press in order to correct errors and improve glosses. For a full list of editorial and typographical corrections made to this edition, please view its correction log on Github: https://github.com/mets-editions/douma-ashby/blob/main/douma-ashby-export-corrections-log.xlsx

youre highnesse Edward . . . So MS. There seems to be another word following the name of Edward, but it is no longer legible. The meter of the line also suggests there should be at least one more syllable in this line. There is a later two-word addition written at the end of this line, in what seems to be a different fifteenth-century, or perhaps later, hand. The first word is clearly by, but the second word is too badly faded for a definitive reading. Bateson reads this addition as by name and includes it in the main text of the stanza (I mene to youre highnesse Edwardes by name), but this cannot be the case. First of all, this addition is not in Ashby’s hand and thus not part of the original text. Secondly, the second word ends in -le. A reconstruction of this line on the basis of the rhyme scheme is not possible, since the last word of line 94 is also illegible.

Hillaritas est intelligendum signum et e contra. So MS. The sense of the Latin phrase here is obscure. The Liber (Franceschini, p. 412) gives more clarity, reading: intelligis que dico? Et respondit: sic; et dixit: non video quod tu intelligas. Respondit discipulus: qualiter vides hoc? Dixit: non video te ylarem, et intelligendi signum est ylaritas. (Do you understand what I am saying? And he responds: yes; and he says: I do not see that you understand it. The pupil responds: how do you see this? And he says: I do not see you cheerful, and cheerfulness is the sign of understanding.) The stanza following this quotation in the Dicta (lines 1101–07) bears little similarity to the meaning of the original passage in the Liber, a didactic exchange interspersed between lessons on tempering anger with patience and the virtue of modesty in children. These lines from which Ashby is quoting here are omitted both by Scrope and by the anonymous translator of the Helmingham Hall manuscript in their Middle English translations of the Dicts and Sayings of the Philosophers (see Bühler, ed., The Dicts and Sayings, pp. 26–27, and Sutton, ed., The Dicts and Sayings, lines 216–28 of 2. Hermes, respectively).

sanctificacionem figurarum. The sense of the Latin is unclear here (the sanctification of the figures?). One manuscript of the Liber (Franceschini, p. 454n8) reads: utere bonis moribus et diligeris, et licet sis turpis, pulcritudo membrorum tuorum occultabit tue fationis figuram (Employ good manners, and you will be loved, and even though you may be ugly, the beauty of your limbs will hide the ugliness of your figure). In this case it seems Ashby’s Latin is more correct in reading morum (manners, habits) instead of membrorum (limbs, members). The Spanish Bocados de Oro, which was translated into Latin in the Liber, reads: la fermosura de tus maneras encobrira la fealdat de tu fechura (Franceschini, p. 453n8) (the beauty of your manners will hide the ugliness of your figure).

after 2178
but so in negligence. The manuscript ends in the middle of this stanza. It is unclear how much text is missing. There is no indication in the poem that Ashby was working towards a conclusion, and because he did not follow the structure of the Liber Philosophorum it is impossible to determine whether he had almost finished working on the source material that he wanted to include. As this folio is the last leaf of a full quire, it is possible that at least a whole quire of the text is missing.
